definition: Machine ethics (or machine morality, computational morality, or computational ethics) is a part of the ethics of artificial intelligence concerned with adding or ensuring moral behaviors of man-made machines that use artificial intelligence (AI), otherwise known as AI agents.
details: Machine ethics differs from other ethical fields related to engineering and technology. It should not be confused with computer ethics, which focuses on human use of computers. It should also be distinguished from the philosophy of technology, which concerns itself with technology's grander social effects.

explainer.lead: Machine ethics is the part of AI ethics concerned with adding or ensuring moral behaviour in man-made machines that use AI, known as AI agents. It matters because it targets the machine's own conduct, not how people use computers.

tiers.eli5: It is about teaching the robot itself to behave well, rather than about how people should use their laptops.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers working on AI agents treat moral behaviour as something to build into the agent. The pitfall is conflating it with computer ethics, which focuses on human use of computers, or with the philosophy of technology, which concerns technology's grander social effects.
tiers.paperLevel: James H. Moor defines four kinds of ethical robots: ethical impact agents, implicit ethical agents, explicit ethical agents, and full ethical agents; a machine may be one or more of these types. Ethical impact agents are systems that carry an ethical impact whether intended or not. The given facts supply no further definitional formalism.

explainer.example: A system whose actions carry ethical consequences whether or not that was intended counts, under Moor's scheme, as an ethical impact agent.
